title: Simon Kimbangu
hookLine: a Congolese healer spends the rest of his life in prison, and a church grows from it

lines: A HEALING, AND THE PATHS FILL.
cards: Nkamba is a village in the hills of the lower Congo. One day, the story goes, a Baptist catechist named Simon Kimbangu lays his hands on a sick woman and prays, and she gets up. Word spreads.
Soon the paths into the village are worn down by people carrying the sick on their backs and on stretchers. Markets empty. Some workers walk off their jobs to go and hear him.
The Belgian colonial officials who run the Congo don't like any of it. A crowd that big, following a Congolese man, looks to them like trouble.

teach.b: Kimbangu's public ministry was short. He preached from the Bible, prayed for the sick, told people to turn from violence and put away old objects of spiritual power, and called them to follow Jesus.
The authorities ordered his arrest. For a while he stayed out of reach.
Then, tradition says, he gave himself up and told his followers not to fight for him.

It echoes that night in Gethsemane, when Jesus said to the disciple who drew a sword, in the King James Bible: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."
A colonial court sentenced him to death.
The sentence was changed to life in prison, and he was taken to a prison at the other end of the country. He never came home. He died there.
Here's the strange part. The man was locked away, his followers watched, some exiled to distant parts of the colony, and the movement didn't vanish. It spread.
Exiled families carried his teaching wherever they were sent.
Out of it grew a church, the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth through the Prophet Simon Kimbangu, which Kimbanguists say grew from his suffering. They honor him as God's prophet.
Other churches describe him in their own ways, and some differ with Kimbanguists about his place. Hebrews asks Christians to remember people in prison, in the King James words, "as bound with them".
For Kimbanguists, the prison isn't where the story ended. It's where the church began.

how: Kimbanguists gather at Nkamba, which they call a holy place, to pray and sing, and they honor Simon Kimbangu as a prophet who suffered for the gospel.

games.why: tradition says he gave himself up and told his followers not to fight, an echo of Jesus telling Peter to put away his sword.

practice: Congo is a huge country of rivers, forests and cities, of families, churches, mosques and markets, and it has known a great deal of suffering.

Picture one family there this evening: a meal cooking, children at homework, someone worried about tomorrow. If you pray, ask peace for that family; if you don't, let your attention rest on them, the way you'd hold a friend's name.

wordCard.voice: Simon Kimbangu. A Congolese catechist and healer who gave himself up, died in a colonial prison, and whose followers built a church.

orig.note: Greek: a prisoner, one in bonds; Paul calls himself the prisoner of Jesus Christ in Ephesians 3:1.

carryVoice: Your line: a church from a prison. What was shut away kept growing. Until tomorrow.
